title: Network Reliability & Observability
summary: Networks fail. Learn to make calls resilient with timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, and fallbacks — then see inside a live system with metrics, logs, and tracing.

blocks.markdown:
Every network call can fail. Reliable services treat failure as the default, not the exception.

- **Timeouts** stop hangs. **Retries** recover from transient errors. **Circuit breakers** stop cascades.
- **Idempotency** makes retries safe. **Fallbacks** keep the user happy when the backend is down.
- **Observability** — metrics, logs, traces — tells you *what* is broken and *why*.
- **SLIs/SLOs** give reliability a number you can act on.

blocks.subTitle: The reliability toolkit at a glance
blocks.markdown:
The tools and what each one guards against.

| Tool | Guards against |
|---|---|
| Timeout | Hanging forever on a slow call |
| Retry + backoff | One-off transient failures |
| Circuit breaker | Hammering a broken downstream |

Observability tools — metrics, logs, traces — let you see failures after they happen.

blocks.subTitle: Fail fast vs hang
blocks.markdown:
A network call has two bad failure modes:

- **Hang** — the call never returns; threads pile up and the whole service stalls.
- **Fast error** — returns a clear error immediately; the caller can handle it and move on.

**Fail fast** is always better than hang. Timeouts turn hangs into fast errors. Without one, a single slow dependency can exhaust your thread pool and take down your service.

A **timeout** is a hard deadline on how long a call may take. Always set one — the default in most HTTP libraries is *infinite*.

- **Connection timeout** — how long to wait to establish the socket (usually 1–5 s).
- **Read timeout** — how long to wait for the first byte after connecting (matches your SLO).
- Set both independently. A connected-but-silent server only triggers the read timeout.

blocks.subTitle: Pitfall: no timeout
blocks.markdown:
**"The library has a default timeout."** Most do not — or the default is unreasonably high (minutes).

- Check the SDK docs. Set both connection and read timeouts explicitly.
- Threads waiting on a hung call hold database connections, file handles, and memory. One slow dependency can cascade to a full outage.
- Budget timeout values from your SLO, not intuition: if your p99 target is 500 ms, set read timeout ≤ 400 ms.

blocks.subTitle: Exponential backoff + jitter
blocks.markdown:
A **retry** resends a failed request. Naive immediate retries amplify load on an already-struggling server.

- **Exponential backoff** — wait grows on each attempt: 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms, 800 ms…
- **Jitter** — add random noise to each wait so many clients do not all retry at the same instant. Without jitter, backoff just synchronises a thundering herd.
- Only retry on **transient** errors (timeout, 503). Never retry 4xx (bad request — retrying won't fix it).

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode

blocks.markdown:
**Idempotency** — running the same operation multiple times has the same effect as running it once.

Retries require it. If a payment request times out mid-flight, did the charge happen? Without idempotency, a retry doubles the charge.

- Use a client-generated **idempotency key** (UUID) per logical request. The server stores it and deduplicates repeats.
- GET and DELETE are naturally idempotent. POST usually is not — make it so explicitly. See [rest-apis-realtime](rest-apis-realtime).

A **circuit breaker** wraps a downstream call. After too many failures it *opens* — requests fail immediately without touching the downstream — letting it recover.

- **Closed** — normal; calls go through.
- **Open** — failing fast; calls blocked. After a cooldown window, a probe request is allowed.
- **Half-open** — testing recovery; one success → Closed, one failure → back to Open.

Pattern from electrical engineering: tripping the breaker before wires burn.

blocks.subTitle: Retry vs circuit breaker
blocks.markdown:
They solve different problems and combine well.

- **Retry** — for *transient* blips (a single bad request). Tries again a few times with backoff.
- **Circuit breaker** — for *sustained* failures. Stops trying entirely until the downstream recovers.

Typical setup: retry inside the circuit breaker. After N consecutive failures the breaker opens — retries stop automatically. See [l4-l7-load-balancing](l4-l7-load-balancing) for how load balancers also shed load.

**Graceful degradation** — when a dependency fails, serve a reduced but still useful response instead of a full error.

- Recommendation service down? Return the static top-10 list from cache.
- Payment gateway slow? Show "try again in a moment" rather than a 500.
- Auth service unavailable? Allow read-only access with cached tokens.

**Fallback** is the concrete implementation: a cached result, a default value, or a simpler code path. Design fallbacks at the start, not during an incident.

blocks.subTitle: The three pillars
blocks.markdown:
**Observability** is the ability to understand a system's internal state from its external outputs. The three pillars:

<<< Image: three equal vertical columns on a shared base labelled 'Observability'. Left column: blue, title 'Metrics', subtitle 'Aggregated numbers over time (p99 latency, error rate, RPS)'. - **Metrics** — *what* is broken (error rate spiked).
- **Logs** — *which* requests failed and with what error.
- **Traces** — *where* in the call chain latency or errors originate.

blocks.subTitle: Distributed tracing
blocks.markdown:
**Distributed tracing** tracks a single request as it hops across microservices.

- Each service adds a **span** (start time, end time, name, service). Spans share a **trace ID** injected into request headers (e.g. `X-Trace-Id`).
- The trace forms a tree: you see exactly which service added latency or failed.
- Tools: Jaeger, Zipkin, AWS X-Ray, OpenTelemetry (the open standard).

Without tracing, debugging latency across 10 services is guesswork. See [network-performance-qos](network-performance-qos).

blocks.subTitle: Health checks and heartbeats
blocks.markdown:
A **health check** is an endpoint (typically `GET /health`) that returns whether the service is ready to handle traffic.

- **Liveness** — is the process alive? Restart if not.
- **Readiness** — is the service ready for traffic? Remove from load balancer if not.
- **Heartbeat** — periodic signal a service sends to a coordinator to prove it is still alive. Missed heartbeats trigger failover.

Load balancers and orchestrators (Kubernetes) poll health endpoints continuously.

blocks.subTitle: SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets
blocks.markdown:
**SLI** (Service Level Indicator) — a measurable metric: e.g. "fraction of requests served in < 200 ms".

**SLO** (Service Level Objective) — a target on that SLI: e.g. "99.9% of requests < 200 ms over 30 days".

**Error budget** — the allowed room to fail: 100% − 99.9% = 0.1% of requests can be slow. Spend the budget on risky deploys; when it runs out, freeze changes and focus on reliability.

SLAs are SLOs with contractual penalties — set SLOs tighter than your SLA.

blocks.subTitle: Why retries need backoff and jitter
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why must retries use exponential backoff *and* jitter?**

Backoff gives the downstream time to recover — immediate retries just add more load to an already-struggling server. Jitter spreads retries across time so all clients do not fire at the same millisecond (the **thundering herd** problem). Backoff without jitter still synchronises clients; jitter without backoff still retries too fast.

blocks.subTitle: Why retries need idempotency
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why do retries require the operation to be idempotent?**

A request can time out *after* the server processed it — the client never got the reply. A retry sends the same request again. If the operation is not idempotent (e.g. charge a card), it executes twice. **Idempotency keys** let the server deduplicate: same key → same result, no double-execution.

blocks.subTitle: What is a circuit breaker
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is a circuit breaker and when does it open?**

A circuit breaker counts failures on calls to a downstream service. When failures exceed a threshold it *opens* — all subsequent calls fail immediately, no network touch. This stops the cascade: your service stays responsive even when the downstream is down. After a cooldown the breaker goes **half-open**: one probe request decides whether to close or stay open.

blocks.subTitle: Three pillars of observability
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What are the three pillars of observability and what does each answer?**

- **Metrics** — aggregate numbers over time. Answer: *what* is wrong (error rate, latency, RPS).
- **Logs** — timestamped records of individual events. Answer: *which* request failed and why.
- **Traces** — the end-to-end path of a request across services. Answer: *where* in the chain the problem is.

Together they let you go from alert → diagnosis → root cause.

blocks.subTitle: SLI vs SLO vs error budget
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Explain SLI, SLO, and error budget for a network service.**

**SLI** is the measurement: "99.5% of API requests completed in < 300 ms this week". **SLO** is the target: "must be ≥ 99.9%". **Error budget** is the gap: 0.1% of requests may be slow before you breach the SLO. Teams spend budget deliberately — risky deploys consume it; when it nears zero, reliability work takes priority over features.
